newsitem.title: USA: Syria, Israel to attend Malta meet, EU envoy says.
newsitem.headline: Syria, Israel to attend Malta meet, EU envoy says.

text.p: Syria has confirmed that it will attend a European-Mediterranean conference in Malta in April that will also be attended by Israel, European Union Middle East envoy Miguel Angel Moratinos said on Monday.

Moratinos told a Washington think-tank that Syrian Foreign Minister Farouq al-Shara, Lebanese Foreign Minister Faris Bouez and Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy were all expected to be at the 27-nation conference opening on April 25.

The meeting is a follow-up to a conference in Barcelona in November 1995 on cooperation between EU and Mediterranean rim countries. A major goal set by that conference was to create a free trade area in industrial goods by 2010.

Syria and Israel were also at Barcelona, but Syria and its ally Lebanon have refused to attend other multilateral conferences on regional issues as part of the U.S.-sponsored Middle East peace process.
Israel broke off direct peace talks with Syria almost a year ago, and fundamental differences over the future of the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights have prevented a resumption.

"The Malta meeting will be at foreign minister level, so Mr. Farouq al-Shara and Mr. Bouez from Lebanon will attend, and David Levy from Israel will attend," Moratinos told the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.

He said Syrian and Israeli officials, as well as businessmen, also were expected to attend a forum on private investment in the European-Mediterranean region in London March 6-7, but it was not yet known at what level.

Moratinos, a Spaniard, said the Barcelona process was "a very important leverage for the whole peace process" and was "the only framework (in which) the Syrians and Lebanese sit together with the Israelis."

Moratinos said after meeting Syrian President Hafez al-Assad on Jan. 29 that Syria was interested in comments by Levy that Israel is ready to resume talks on the basis of the 1991 Madrid peace conference and U.N. resolutions, but that Damascus wanted more details.

But the EU envoy, who is in Washington to confer with his U.S. counterpart Dennis Ross, said on Monday the Israeli-Syrian situation was "still very difficult" and there appeared no prospect of talks resuming soon.

Syria wants to resume the talks on the basis of what it says was a commitment by Israel's former Labour government to withdraw from the Golan, but the current Likud government has refused to embrace Labour's "land-for-peace" concept.
